reading.body:
Governance, not raw capability, is the distinguishing feature across this set of enterprise AI platforms: nearly every tool in this category surfaces access controls, audit logs, permission-aware retrieval, or compliance hosting as a primary selling point.

The pattern reflects where enterprise adoption stalls. Deploying an AI agent inside a large organization requires answers to questions about who can see what data, how decisions are logged, and whether the system meets regional data-residency rules. Kore.ai lists RBAC, audit logs, and guardrails explicitly. Glean builds permission-awareness into retrieval at the connector level. Cognigy advertises GDPR compliance and EU-hosted infrastructure. These are not peripheral features; they are the conditions under which procurement approves a purchase order.

The data covers eight vendors, seven US-headquartered and one German, so it does not represent the full global market. The notes are brief and vendor-reported, which means capability claims are unverified and comparative depth is limited. Nothing in this data speaks to the underlying compute infrastructure these platforms consume or depend on, so no inference about power or grid demand is warranted here. What the data does show clearly is that the enterprise segment has moved past the question of whether agents work and arrived at the question of whether they can be controlled.
